Impact materialisation description:
In late May 2025, the forced repatriation of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, triggering a growing humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan. Since Pakistan’s crackdown on undocumented foreigners in September 2023, over 850,000 Afghans have been deported or have returned under pressure, with daily arrivals now averaging between 7,000–10,000 individuals. In response to the mounting crisis, the Afghan authorities, in collaboration with international humanitarian organisations, have launched an Integrated Response Plan for Returnees. This initiative aims to address both immediate needs – such as shelter, food, and medical assistance – and long-term reintegration challenges, including livelihood support and legal documentation.
Despite this, the situation remains dire. Upon arrival, most returnees are received in temporary camps that are already overcrowded and underresourced. In many cases, several families are forced to share a single tent. Access to clean water, sanitation, and healthcare is severely limited, heightening health risks, particularly among children and older people.
Women and girls face some of the harshest consequences of the return. An estimated 150,000 school-age girls have returned since the crackdown began, most of whom remain barred from attending school owing to Taliban-imposed restrictions. Women-headed households, in particular, face heightened economic insecurity, as women are banned from working in most sectors, severely limiting their ability to provide for their families.
Children are also critically affected. Reports indicate that over 250,000 children returning from Pakistan are in urgent need of shelter, food, and education. Approximately 65% of them are currently not enrolled in school, primarily given a lack of documentation or gender-based restrictions. Alarmingly, 99% of returnee families report insufficient food to last more than a few weeks.
Human rights defenders, former government workers, and those with ties to foreign military forces face serious protection risks, including arbitrary detention and persecution. There are also widespread reports of abuse, including extortion by Pakistani authorities during detention and deportation processes.
Projections suggest that if Pakistan’s deportation campaign continues unchecked, tens of thousands more will be forced to return, potentially overwhelming Afghanistan’s already fragile infrastructure and deepening its humanitarian crisis.

Risk Title: La Niña in Afghanistan worsens drought and leads to widespread agricultural losses, water scarcity, and acute food insecurity in 2026
Rationale:
In Afghanistan, La Niña conditions started in October 2025 and are likely to persist until the February–March 2026 period. La Niña typically brings below-normal snowfall and rainfall combined with above-average temperatures in the country, driving drought-like conditions that significantly degrade agricultural productivity and water availability. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions face a heightened risk of both agricultural and hydrological drought, directly threatening food security and rural livelihoods for farming and pastoralist communities. The current agricultural deficit reflects cumulative climate stress. In the 2024–2025 period, Afghanistan faced its fourth consecutive season of below-average production, with documented crop failures across eastern and northern areas. Dry conditions are likely to affect 2025 second-season crops (rice, cotton, and maize), most of which are harvested at the end of October, while forecasted below-average winter precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 is likely to affect winter wheat production in 2026. Dry conditions also heighten concerns about fodder availability, likely affecting households dependent on pastoral income.
Below-average winter rainfall and snowfall are expected to curtail water availability in spring/summer, limiting irrigation, pasture growth, and snowmelt-fed rivers vital for agriculture and drinking water. Agricultural stress and water scarcity will compound the impact of recent seismic events. A series of earthquakes in 2025 destroyed homes and water/sanitation infrastructure while displacing tens of thousands, simultaneously triggering emergency shelter and WASH needs. Earthquake impacts, layered atop drought and flood shocks, have dramatically increased pressure on already-stretched community resources and humanitarian response. Population movements further intensify pressure on resources; over 2.6 million Afghans have returned from Iran and Pakistan since January 2025. These overlapping movements place severe strain on basic services, employment opportunities, and social cohesion in hosting communities, particularly in water-stressed border provinces. ([FEWS NET et al. 07/02/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/07401c1b-0f71-46d4-810c-5e4e3a6064d1/2025_01_Afghanistan.pdf), [Mercy Corps 08/10/2025](https://www.mercycorps.org/press-room/releases/Crisis-Compounded-Afghanistan), [Alcis 01/07/2025](https://www.alcis.org/post/crop-estimates-for-six-provinces-in-afghanistan), [FEWS NET 06/10/2025](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/afghanistan/key-message-update/september-2025), [FSC 02/2025](https://fscluster.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Afghanistan%20EWIWG%20-%20Key%20messages%20Feb%202025.pdf))

Additionally, spring water availability is significantly constrained because of weak snowpack and reduced snowmelt. Risk Title: Continued attacks between Pakistan and Afghanistan increase protection risks, food security needs, and access constraints in Afghanistan’s border provinces
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps. ([CFR 18/03/2026](https://www.cfr.org/articles/why-are-the-afghan-taliban-and-pakistan-in-an-open-war), [The Guardian 29/06/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/29/pakistan-deadly-airstrikes-afghanistan-border), [HRW 15/07/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/07/15/pakistani-strikes-in-afghanistan-raise-civilian-casualty-concerns), [UNAMA 11/05/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/English%20-%20UNAMA%20HRS%20paper%20on%20cross-border%20civilian%20casualties%20-%20Jan-Mar%202026_Updated_11.05.26.pdf), [WFP 26/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/food-security-under-pressure-impacts-middle-east-crisis-and-pakistan-conflict-afghanistan-june-2026), [OCHA 28/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-situation-update-4-humanitarian-impact-afghanistan-pakistan-military-escalation-28-april-2026), [NPR 03/04/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/03/g-s1-116299/pakistan-says-a-new-round-of-peace-talks-with-afghanistan-is-underway-in-china), [Reuters 02/04/2026](https://www.aol.com/articles/pakistan-says-talks-afghanistan-end-071917568.html), [UNAMA 29/06/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/en/news/unama-statement-on-civilian-casualties))

Afghanistan–Pakistan transit trade has suffered one of its steepest declines, plunging to just 11,592 containers worth USD 367 million in the outgoing fiscal year from nearly 89,000 containers valued at USD 5 billion before the Taliban returned to power, as Kabul’s growing reliance on Iranian routes and Pakistan’s border curbs reshaped the decades-old trade corridor. Continued conflict and border closures are likely to further restrict trade and humanitarian supply flows over the next three to six months, compounding food insecurity in affected provinces.
Communities in bordering areas are dealing with a scarcity of food and essential services. People are often forced to implement potentially harmful coping mechanisms, such as child marriage in exchange for food and money.
Pakistan continues to serve as Afghanistan's primary overland transit route for international humanitarian assistance, and the conflict escalation further restricts access for humanitarian aid. Only until 13 July, Pakistani customs authorities issued gate passes for 26 containers carrying food and essential relief supplies after completing customs formalities. The latest clearance does not signal a reopening of the crossing but provides a limited humanitarian exemption to facilitate UN relief operations. ([PRIO 28/05/2026](https://www.prio.org/comments/1887), [OCHA accessed 17/07/2026](https://www.unocha.org/afghanistan), [UN 13/05/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/05/1167500), [Dawn 19/07/2026](https://www.dawn.com/news/2016605), [AnewZ 14/07/2026](https://anewz.tv/region/south-asia/21822/pakistan-allows-un-aid-convoy-into-afghanistan/news))
Expected impact:
Populations along the Durand Line will experience high protection risks. Civilian casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, particularly in border-adjacent provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, and Paktika), will likely occur. There is also a high risk of damage to civilian infrastructure, homes, markets, and health facilities, reducing safe access to essential services.
An estimated 21.9 million people are in need across Afghanistan in 2026, including 15 million in need of protection and 4.2 million in need of shelter and site management support. This figure may not account for the estimated 500,000 conflict-displaced people.
The conflict is likely to impede access to services, deteriorate the livelihoods of people, particularly returnees recently reported from Pakistan and Iran. There were over 2.5 million returnees from Iran and Pakistan in 2025, adding pressure on overstretched local resources, services, and livelihoods. 
Forced displacement is expected to persist and is likely to increase, causing a deterioration of humanitarian needs in provinces along the Durand Line. In April 2026 alone, over 9,000 families were forced to leave their homes given the rocket attacks conducted by Pakistani forces on areas near the Durand Line in Afghanistan’s Kunar province.
The provinces of Kunar, Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika are projected to remain in Stressed (IPC Phase 2) food security conditions or deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the lean season. Paktika has been among the most affected provinces, experiencing repeated cross-border shelling that has damaged civilian infrastructure and displaced communities, reducing access to health services and agricultural livelihoods. The situation is partly caused by the prolonged closure of key Durand Line crossings, impeding the trade and import of food and directly affecting food security and livelihoods in Afghanistan. Growing uncertainty around commodity movements through Iran because of the volatile Middle East conflict is also driving up logistics costs and reducing the availability of essential goods in local markets. Further conflict escalation along the Durand Line is likely to  delay any reopening of border crossings and halt the limited humanitarian convoys currently permitted through, further reducing the availability of essential goods and deepening food insecurity.
The direct impact of conflict escalation on civilian protection and humanitarian access is expected to be the primary driver of increased need. Casualties, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access caused by persistent air strikes and border closures are likely to push additional populations into IPC 3 before food insecurity peaks. Up to 2.3 million additional people could become food-insecure as a result of a prolonged border closure with Pakistan and further conflict escalation. At the same time, food assistance currently reaches only 2.7% of the population because of governmental restrictions and funding shortfalls.
By October 2026, the depletion of household harvest stocks and the seasonal decline in agricultural labour will increase market dependence just as conflict-driven border closures at Torkham are expected to drive prices upwards through the lean season peak from December–January. The situation is compounded by high unemployment and declining remittance inflows. Risk Title: Escalating clashes between Interim Taliban Authority forces and armed opposition groups in Badakhshan deteriorates food security and increases protection risks
Rationale:
Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook. Current vulnerability / Coping capacitie:
The entire Badakhshan province is currently experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity levels according to FEWS NET, but IPC assessments place it in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through the current period.
The wheat harvest is still in its early stages as harvesting begins later at higher elevations. The delay in harvest impedes households’ access to harvest-related food and income and keeps them reliant on market purchases in the meantime. Staple food prices are elevated by the high cost of transport to these remote areas, while household income is further constrained by below-average labour opportunities. Poor households in the province are already reporting food consumption gaps and depleting assets; intensified conflict would likely accelerate this depletion by disrupting markets, movement, and livelihoods, pushing more households towards potentially harmful coping strategies.
Above-average precipitation – in the form of increased snowfall at higher elevations and increased rain and snow at lower elevations, particularly between October–April – is expected, and this is plausibly positive for the harvest, improving water availability after several drought-affected seasons. On the other hand, favourable weather conditions may fail to translate into higher production if farmers are unable to access fertiliser before and during the autumn planting period amid rising prices.
There is limited information about health in the province, although communities have reported shortages of medicines and adequate facilities; there are also reports of substance use in place of unavailable medicines. In July 2026, the Health Cluster reported reaching around 5,300 people in the province. Badakhshan's mountainous terrain also imposes deep access constraints on humanitarian response, meaning any increase in clashes is likely to further restrict access to affected populations.
Recently, the province experienced floods in Shughnan and Maimai districts. Floods damaged schools, 42,800 hectares of cultivated agricultural land, and other critical infrastructure, including bridges and water mills, as well as killing livestock. Flash floods may have displaced explosive ordnance or exposed previous landmines. Expected impact:
Intensified conflict would directly affect communities' protection, with people likely exposed to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and the risk of casualties. Repeated fighting over district centres could trigger short- and medium-term displacement as families flee active front lines, restricting mobility and disrupting livelihoods in turn.
Gold mining disputes between armed groups have disrupted local livelihoods. The ITA has suspended mining in contested areas to cut off income for opposition armed groups, in the process also stripping income from mining-dependent communities, which are not necessarily tied to armed groups. Badakhshan's mines department head reported around 650–700 mining companies, with thousands of people working manually. Thousands of miners are specifically deployed in areas such as Shiwa. Further escalation could mean lost income for miners caught between Taliban control efforts and dissident commanders. Health access, already limited, would likely deteriorate further; communities have already reported shortages of medicines and adequate facilities, as well as substance use in place of unavailable medicines. Escalating conflict increases the risk of health facilities being damaged, occupied, or forced to suspend services and could disrupt the already-limited supply of medicines to clinics.
This livelihood pressure is set against a difficult seasonal outlook. Above-average precipitation expected between October 2026 and April 2027 could damage the upcoming harvest, further eroding food security just as the lean season approaches. Food prices are already rising, and further disruption to markets, movement, and livelihoods could push households towards potentially harmful coping strategies, such as early marriage and skipping meals.
The current context in Badakhshan points to a compounding risk: rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating health and food security outlook. Risk Title: Resource-related clashes and political tensions in Tindouf camps restrict humanitarian access and increase protection risks for Sahrawi refugees
Rationale:
The risk of increased instability and localised clashes in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, may rise over the coming months as humanitarian pressures, political uncertainty, and governance challenges compound a protracted displacement crisis.  

Several incidents between April–June 2026 suggest growing tensions within the camps. On 20 April, armed confrontations involving Polisario-linked elements and the Algerian National Army over humanitarian aid distribution highlighted tensions related to influence, compounded by the lack of resources. On 28 April, clashes between members of the Fakra and Oulad Moussa tribes in Smara camp escalated from a dispute over access to a water tap into armed confrontations involving live ammunition. The violence resulted in injuries and damage to tents, houses, and vehicles, raising concerns about the capacity of camp authorities to manage local disputes and prevent escalation. 

In this context, tensions are most likely to unfold through repeated, low-level disputes between tribes, families, or Polisario-affiliated actors in camps such as Smara, Laayoune, Awserd, and Dakhla, particularly around water points, aid distribution systems, and local administrative structures. These disputes are likely to remain contained but may escalate into short-lived violent incidents when mediation fails or when armed actors become involved. 

Political developments have further increased uncertainty and may be contributing to growing confusion and frustration among refugee populations regarding future governance arrangements. On 22 April, reports indicated increased US pressure on Algeria regarding the future of the Tindouf camps and the Western Sahara conflict. On 29 May, concerns emerged among Polisario supporters over a perceived shift in Algeria's position on negotiations. On 9 June, the death of senior Polisario commander Lahbib Mohamed Abdelaziz in a reported drone strike fuelled speculation regarding future leadership dynamics within the movement. 

Although these developments have not triggered widespread unrest, they indicate increasing pressure on camp governance, resource management, and political cohesion. Further reductions in humanitarian assistance, deterioration in living conditions, or renewed political tensions surrounding Western Sahara could increase the likelihood of additional intercommunal violence, protests, or localised instability within the camps over the next 6–12 months. ([ACLED accessed 18/06/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool\), [UNHCR 27/11/2025](https://algeria.un.org/fr/306201-plan-de-r%C3%A9ponse-pour-les-r%C3%A9fugi%C3%A9s-sahraouis-2026%E2%80%932027\), [Africanews 23/04/2026](https://www.africanews.com/2026/04/23/in-algerian-desert-sahrawi-refugees-still-dream-of-independent-homeland/), [Atalayar 22/04/2026](https://www.atalayar.com/en/articulo/politics/the-united-states-is-putting-pressure-on-algeria-and-urging-it-to-dismantle-the-tindouf-camps/20260422210000225067.html), [Algeria Times 20/04/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75054\), [Yabiladi 29/04/2026](https://en.yabiladi.com/articles/details/193455/violent-clashes-tindouf-s-smara-camp.html\), [Barlaman Today 30/04/2026](https://barlamantoday.com/2026/04/30/deadly-armed-clashes-reportedly-erupt-in-tindouf-camps/), [Assahifa 29/05/2026](https://www.assahifa.com/%D8%B9%D9%82%D8%A8-%D8%BA%D8%B6%D8%A8-%D9%85%D8%AE%D9%8A%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B1-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%B7%D9%85%D8%A3/), [Algeria Times 11/06/2026](https://algeriatimes.net/detail/view/75662\), [Belpresse 09/06/2026](https://www.belpresse.com/politique/%d9%85%d9%82%d8%aa%d9%84-%d9%86%d8%ac%d9%84-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b2%d8%b9%d9%8a%d9%85-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%a8%d9%82-%d9%84%d9%84%d8%a8%d9%88%d9%84%d9%8a%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%b1%d9%8a%d9%88-%d9%8a%d8%b6/)).

Risk Title: Prolonged fuel shortages in Bangladesh worsen food security and disrupt health, telecommunications, and other essential services
Risk Type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
Rationale:
Geopolitical shocks, import dependency, and market distortions risk a prolonged or widespread fuel shortage across Bangladesh, worsening the humanitarian situation. The country imports about 95% of its petroleum – 63% from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates via the Strait of Hormuz. The 2026 war between Israel–US and Iran has disrupted this corridor, constraining imports; continued disruptions would further limit fuel supply. Despite diversifying imports towards the US after a February 2026 trade deal, alternative routes are unable to replace Middle Eastern volumes at scale, leaving near-term shortfall risks.
Bangladesh's capacity to absorb disruptions is eroding as economic conditions worsen. Inflation reached 9.13% in February 2026, and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation import costs rose by 29% year-on-year. Pressure on foreign exchange reserves, including reduced remittance inflows from the Gulf countries affected by the war, may constrain fuel imports. Distribution practices – hoarding, panic-buying, and first-come-first-served allocation – further limit access.
These supply constraints are converging with peak seasonal demand during Boro season – the December–May dry-season rice cultivation period that accounts for around 55% of annual production. Should fuel shortages persist through this period, the consequences for food security are likely to be severe. Limited diesel availability and government policies such as a two-litre-per-visit rationing cap are constraining irrigation, especially in northern districts, where demand exceeds supply. Farmers report shortages of both diesel and electricity.
